newsitem.title: ALBANIA: Albania appeals for military help to end anarchy.
newsitem.headline: Albania appeals for military help to end anarchy.

text.p: Albania's beleaguered government called for foreign military intervention on Thursday to halt spreading disorder as the United States and European nations evacuated nationals from the Balkan state.

In an initial reaction to the desperate call from Tirana, German Chancellor Helmut Kohl said the Albanian crisis was essentially an internal matter and it was not clear what foreign troops would do there.
Spain, however, said it would contribute a military force if it had the support of other European nations.

As Europe attempted to coordinate its response to a fresh Balkan flareup less than two years after war ended in Bosnia, the United States sent four U.S. Chinook 46 military helicopters into Tirana to pull out its nationals.
Shooting and looting spread to Tirana following two weeks of armed insurrection in towns in the south.
About 50 Americans, most of them children, had already been ferried out of the country to U.S. ships standing offshore, U.S. State Department spokesman Nicholas Burns said.
The operation would go on until 170 non-essential embassy employees, their dependants and those among 2,000 other Americans wanting to leave had been air-lifted to safety, he said.

-- Italy rescued some 400 foreign nationals with helicopters and ferried them to Italian warships in the Adriatic. Diplomatic sources said the evacuees included about 330 Italians and some 70 other foreigners.

-- Britain organised a pullout of some 100 foreign nationals in a convoy of vehicles from Tirana to the port of Durres. The Foreign Office said 65 British nationals, 52 people of other nationalities, 11 Commonwealth citizens and three from Ireland had arrived at the port ready for evacuation to Italy.
-- Greece and Austria said they were preparing evacuations of their nationals, and Hungary and Bulgaria were also reported to be doing the same.

In the clearest sign yet that President Sali Berisha and the newly-formed coalition government were no longer in control, all political parties urged NATO's European members to use their military to end the turmoil.
Civilians in Tirana, apparently intent on defending themselves in the face of a complete breakdown of civil order, ransacked arms depots while police vanished from the streets.

All political forces in Albania agreed that outside military assistance was needed "to restore the constitutional order and to preserve the country's integrity", the government said in an appeal sent to the Western European Union (WEU).
The WEU, considered the future defence arm of the European Union, includes Britain, France, Germany and Italy.
Responses to the call were varied while diplomatic efforts to stop anarchy turning to conflict gathered pace.
In the Hague, Dutch Foreign Minister Hans van Mierlo, whose country currently holds the EU presidency, said the EU was seriously considering the request.

But German Chancellor Helmut Kohl told reporters after talks with Dutch Prime Minister Wim Kok that the crisis was largely an internal affair and it was not clear what Western troops would do in Albania if sent there to help restore order.
EU foreign ministers are due to meet this weekend in the Dutch town of Apeldoorn for informal talks which are likely to focus on deepening Albanian crisis.
NATO, expressing great worry over the turmoil, said it was watching events there closely but gave no indication it was considering plans for military intervention.
In New York, Italy and Albania asked for an emergency meeting of the U.N. Security Council, urging the 15-member body to issue a statement before possible massacres break out.

A mission of the Organisation for Security and Cooperation in Europe led by former Austrian chancellor Franz Vranitzky was due to leave from Vienna on an Italian military plane at 6 a.m. (0500 GMT) on Friday morning for Bari. Helicopters would fly the 10-member delegation either to the Albanian mainland or an Italian ship for talks with political leaders and rebel representatives.

A declaration of a state of emergency by the Albanian parliament nearly two weeks ago, and warnings that security forces would shoot to kill, did nothing to halt the insurrection. Armed rebellion erupted following weeks of protests by ordinary Albanians who lost their meagre savings in shady pyramid investment schemes and who blamed Berisha and the former government led by his Democratic Party.
Attempts to control the insurgency by deploying the army, secret police and regular police forces have failed, with signs of desertion by security forces on the increase.
-- Two Albanian air force helicopters with several people on board landed near the Italian port of Brindisi and military sources in Rome said four more had been sighted heading for Italy.
-- The Italian navy said three Albanian torpedo boats had deserted in international waters where they raised the white flag of surrender after being sighted by an Italian frigate.

-- Violence reached the northern border as seven Albanian border policemen trying to cross the frontier with Macedonia at Kjafasan engaged in a firefight with Macedonian border guards. The Albanians later fled and no one was reported injured.
Yugoslavia closed its border with Albania and raised the degree of combat readiness of some army units on its southern frontier.
